title: Orbit, Nose, Ear, Mouth & Throat
summary: The compact special regions of the head: their walls, contents and nerve supply.

lessons.title: Bony Orbit, Extraocular Muscles & the Orbital Apex

levels.kid:
Your eyes sit in two bony cups in your skull called **orbits**. Each cup is shaped like an ice cream cone lying on its side. The wide part faces forward, and the pointy tip points back toward your brain.

Seven bones join together to make each cup. Some of the walls are thick and strong. Others are as thin as an eggshell!

Six tiny muscles hold each eye, like the strings on a puppet. They pull the eye up, down, left, right, and even twist it a little.

At the pointy back of the cone are small holes. Nerves and blood vessels pass through them, like wires going through a hole in a wall. The biggest one is the **optic nerve**, which carries pictures from your eye to your brain.
levels.hs:
The **orbit** is the bony socket that holds the eye. It is shaped like a four-sided pyramid. Its base is the opening at the front, and its tip, the **apex**, points backward toward the brain.

Seven bones build each orbit: frontal, zygomatic, maxilla, sphenoid, ethmoid, lacrimal and palatine. The walls are:
- **Roof**: mostly frontal bone, with the brain's frontal lobe just above it.
- **Lateral wall**: zygomatic and sphenoid bones. This is the thickest wall.
- **Floor**: mostly maxilla, sitting over the maxillary sinus.
- **Medial wall**: largely the paper-thin ethmoid bone (the **lamina papyracea**).

Six **extraocular muscles** move the eye. Four are **rectus** muscles (superior, inferior, medial, lateral). Two are **oblique** muscles (superior and inferior). A seventh muscle, the levator palpebrae superioris, lifts the upper eyelid.

Three cranial nerves control these muscles. A classic memory rule is **LR6 SO4, all the rest 3**:
- The lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve (CN VI).
- The superior oblique is supplied by the trochlear nerve (CN IV).
- All the others are supplied by the oculomotor nerve (CN III).

Real example: a punch to the eye can crack the thin floor in a **blowout fracture**. The inferior rectus can then get trapped in the break, so the person sees double when looking up.
levels.college:
**Walls and openings.** The orbit is a pyramid of seven bones. Its weakest walls are the medial wall (the ethmoid's lamina papyracea) and the floor (maxilla, weakest along the infraorbital groove). These are the classic fracture sites. The roof separates the orbit from the anterior cranial fossa. The lateral wall is the strongest, but it is also the most exposed.

Key apertures:
- **Optic canal** (lesser wing of sphenoid): carries the optic nerve (CN II) and the ophthalmic artery.
- **Superior orbital fissure (SOF)**, between the greater and lesser wings: carries CN III, IV, V1 (lacrimal, frontal, nasociliary), VI, and the superior ophthalmic vein.
- **Inferior orbital fissure**: carries the infraorbital and zygomatic nerves, plus branches of the inferior ophthalmic vein.
- **Anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina**: carry the ethmoidal vessels and nerves.

**The muscles.** The four recti and the superior oblique arise from the apex. The recti take origin from the **common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn)**, which surrounds the optic canal and the central part of the SOF. The inferior oblique is the exception: it arises anteriorly, from the orbital floor near the lacrimal fossa.

Primary actions (from primary gaze):
- Medial rectus: adduction. Lateral rectus: abduction.
- Superior rectus: elevation, adduction, intorsion.
- Inferior rectus: depression, adduction, extorsion.
- Superior oblique: intorsion, depression, abduction. Its tendon passes through the **trochlea**, a fibrocartilage pulley.
- Inferior oblique: extorsion, elevation, abduction.

The orbit's axis diverges about 23° from the visual axis. Because of this, the vertical recti act purely as elevator and depressor when the eye is abducted. The obliques act purely as depressor and elevator when the eye is adducted. This is the basis of the clinical **H-test**.

**Nerve palsies.**
- CN VI palsy: the eye turns inward (esotropia).
- CN IV palsy: vertical diplopia, worse on looking down, for example when reading or descending stairs. Patients often tilt the head away from the affected side.
- CN III palsy: the eye sits 'down and out', with ptosis, and often a dilated pupil.
levels.phd:
**Annulus and compartments.** The common tendinous ring divides the SOF into compartments, and this division predicts the deficits seen with lesions.

- **Within the ring (oculomotor foramen):** the superior and inferior divisions of CN III, the nasociliary nerve, CN VI, and the sympathetic root to the ciliary ganglion.
- **Above and lateral to the ring:** the lacrimal and frontal nerves, CN IV and the superior ophthalmic vein.

This explains why CN IV can survive some intraconal lesions. It also explains why frontal-nerve anesthesia separates superolateral SOF pathology from intraconal disease.

**The ciliary ganglion** lies lateral to the optic nerve, near the apex. Its parasympathetic root comes from the inferior division of CN III, carrying Edinger–Westphal fibers that travel with the nerve to the inferior oblique. These fibers innervate the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle via the short ciliary nerves. Pupillomotor fibers run superficially and dorsomedially in the cisternal CN III. This is the anatomical basis of the 'pupil rule': compressive lesions such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm involve the pupil early, whereas ischemic microvascular palsy usually spares it.

**Pulley theory.** Demer's high-resolution MRI work in the 1990s–2000s showed connective-tissue **pulleys** that stabilize the paths of the rectus muscles. These pulleys make the effective origin functional rather than purely bony, and they help explain Listing's law and the commutativity of eye rotations. Demer also proposed an 'active pulley hypothesis', in which each muscle has an orbital layer inserting on the pulley and a global layer inserting on the globe. This remains debated, particularly whether the oblique pulley moves actively in a neurally coordinated way.

**Fiber specialization.** Extraocular muscle is unusual. It is among the fastest and most fatigue-resistant skeletal muscle and contains **multiply innervated fibers**. It expresses distinctive myosins, including EOM-specific and embryonic isoforms. Its motor units are very small, which permits precise control. These properties partly explain why EOM is involved early in myasthenia gravis yet relatively spared in Duchenne dystrophy.

**Spatial constraint.** Orbital volume is about 30 mL, and the globe occupies about 7 mL. The septum and bony walls make the orbit a near-closed compartment, so small volume increases sharply raise pressure.
levels.expert:
**Orbital apex syndromes.** The localization logic follows the compartments described above:
- **SOF syndrome:** CN III, IV, VI and V1 deficits.
- **Orbital apex syndrome:** the same deficits plus optic neuropathy.
- **Cavernous sinus syndrome:** the same deficits, possibly with V2 involvement and Horner's syndrome, but usually without early optic involvement.

The causes are broad: invasive fungal sinusitis (mucormycosis, Aspergillus), IgG4-related disease, Tolosa–Hunt syndrome, sphenoid wing meningioma, lymphoma and metastasis. Diagnoses of exclusion such as Tolosa–Hunt should be accepted only after biopsy or follow-up imaging, because corticosteroid responsiveness does not exclude lymphoma.

**Emergencies.** **Retrobulbar hemorrhage** with orbital compartment syndrome requires lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis, usually within about 90–120 minutes. It is a clinical decision and should not be delayed for imaging. Orbital floor fractures in children can produce a 'white-eyed blowout': a trapdoor fracture entraps the inferior rectus with little external bruising. It can trigger the oculocardiac reflex, causing bradycardia, nausea and syncope, and needs urgent release to prevent muscle ischemia.

**Surgical corridors.** Neurosurgeons approach the apex through several routes:
- **Transcranial:** pterional or orbitozygomatic approaches with optic canal unroofing and removal of the anterior clinoid.
- **Endoscopic endonasal:** medial orbital and optic canal decompression through the lamina papyracea and lesser wing. The ophthalmic artery typically lies inferolateral to the nerve in the canal, so the medial optic canal is opened cautiously.
- **Transorbital neuroendoscopic surgery (TONES):** for example the superior eyelid route to the lateral orbit, middle fossa and cavernous sinus. This is a rapidly growing frontier.

Key hazards include the **ethmoidal arteries**, which are landmarks for the skull base level; a dehiscent lamina papyracea; and an Onodi (sphenoethmoidal) cell that places the optic nerve within the posterior ethmoid.

**Imaging pitfalls.** Thyroid eye disease enlarges the muscle bellies while sparing the tendons, typically in the order inferior, medial, superior, then lateral. Orbital myositis, by contrast, tends to involve the tendons. Apical crowding in thyroid eye disease can cause compressive optic neuropathy even when proptosis is mild. Teprotumumab (an IGF-1R antibody) has changed medical management, with open questions about durability and hearing toxicity.

**Open questions** include the active pulley mechanics, the precise anatomy of the superior oblique's relationship to the trochlear nerve, and how much surgical strabismus outcomes depend on manipulating the pulleys.

keyPoints: The orbit is a seven-bone pyramid; the medial wall and floor are thinnest
The optic canal carries CN II and the ophthalmic artery
The superior orbital fissure carries CN III, IV, V1, VI and the superior ophthalmic vein
Four recti and the superior oblique arise at the apex; the inferior oblique arises anteriorly
LR6 SO4, all the rest 3: the nerve supply of the eye muscles
Apex syndrome = SOF deficits plus optic neuropathy

test.q: Which orbital wall contains the paper-thin lamina papyracea?
test.explain: The lamina papyracea is part of the ethmoid bone and forms most of the medial wall. The lateral wall is the thickest.

test.q: Which nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle?
test.explain: LR6: the lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve, CN VI.

test.q: What passes through the optic canal along with the optic nerve?
test.explain: The optic canal carries CN II and the ophthalmic artery. The vein and the other nerves listed travel through the superior orbital fissure.

test.q: Which extraocular muscle does not arise from the orbital apex?
test.explain: The inferior oblique arises anteriorly, from the orbital floor. The recti and the superior oblique originate at the apex.

test.q: A blowout fracture of the floor most often traps which muscle?
test.explain: The inferior rectus lies on the floor and can be caught in the fracture, causing double vision on upgaze.

test.q: A complete CN III palsy typically leaves the eye positioned:
test.explain: The unopposed lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) pull the eye down and out.

test.q: Vertical double vision that worsens when going down stairs suggests a palsy of:
test.explain: A CN IV palsy weakens the superior oblique, which depresses the eye, especially when it is adducted, as in reading or descending stairs.

test.q: The common tendinous ring is also called the:
test.explain: The annulus of Zinn is the origin of the four recti. The trochlea is the pulley for the superior oblique tendon.

test.q: Which structure passes through the superior orbital fissure?
test.explain: CN VI passes through the SOF. The optic nerve and ophthalmic artery use the optic canal, and the infraorbital nerve uses the inferior orbital fissure.

test.q: What is the name of the fibrocartilage pulley that the superior oblique tendon passes through?
test.explain: The trochlea redirects the superior oblique's pull, which gives the trochlear nerve its name.

test.q: An abducens palsy turns the eye inward, a deviation called ___.
test.explain: Without the lateral rectus, the medial rectus pulls the eye inward.

test.q: How many bones form each orbit?
test.explain: The seven bones are the frontal, zygomatic, maxilla, sphenoid, ethmoid, lacrimal and palatine.

kidTest.q: What shape is the eye socket like?
kidTest.explain: The orbit is like a sideways ice cream cone, wide at the front and pointy at the back.

kidTest.q: How many muscles move each eye?
kidTest.explain: Six small muscles pull the eye in different directions.

kidTest.q: What does the optic nerve carry?
kidTest.explain: The optic nerve sends what you see to your brain.

kidTest.q: What are the eye muscles like?
kidTest.explain: The muscles pull the eye like strings pull a puppet.

kidTest.q: The bony cup that holds your eye is called the o _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Each eye sits in an orbit.

advancedTest.q: A lesion causes ophthalmoplegia and V1 numbness with normal vision. Adding optic neuropathy would move the localization to:
choices: The cavernous sinus, behind the apex
advancedTest.explain: Orbital apex syndrome is SOF syndrome plus optic neuropathy, because the optic canal sits right beside the fissure at the apex.

advancedTest.q: Why does a posterior communicating artery aneurysm usually involve the pupil in CN III palsy?
choices: The pupillary fibers lie superficially on the nerve
The pupillary fibers run deep in the core of the nerve
The pupillary fibers travel in the abducens nerve
The aneurysm blocks the ciliary ganglion directly
advancedTest.explain: Superficial pupillomotor fibers are compressed early. Ischemic palsy damages the core of the nerve and so tends to spare them.

advancedTest.q: To isolate the elevating action of the superior rectus clinically, the eye should first be:
advancedTest.explain: In about 23° of abduction, the visual axis aligns with the muscle's line of pull, so the superior rectus acts as a pure elevator.

advancedTest.q: On CT, enlarged inferior and medial recti with tendon sparing most favor:
advancedTest.explain: Thyroid eye disease enlarges the muscle bellies while sparing the tendons, typically inferior and medial first. Myositis tends to involve the tendons.

lessons.title: Nasal Cavity, Paranasal Sinuses & Drainage Pathways

levels.kid:
Your nose is more than two holes on your face. Behind it is a big tunnel called the **nasal cavity**, split down the middle by a thin wall.

On each side wall are three curly shelves. They work like radiators. They warm the air you breathe and make it damp before it reaches your lungs.

Around your nose, inside the bones of your face, are hollow spaces called **sinuses**. They are like little caves full of air. They make your head lighter and help your voice sound full.

Each cave has a tiny door that lets mucus drain into your nose. When you have a cold, those doors can swell shut. Then mucus gets stuck, and your face feels stuffy and sore.
levels.hs:
The **nasal cavity** runs from the nostrils back to the **choanae**, the openings into the throat (nasopharynx). A midline **nasal septum**, made of cartilage in front and thin bone behind, divides it into left and right sides.

The side (lateral) walls carry three scroll-shaped bones called **conchae** (or turbinates): superior, middle and inferior. They create turbulence so air touches warm, moist, mucus-covered lining. The groove under each concha is a **meatus**, and that is where things drain.

The **paranasal sinuses** are air-filled spaces in four skull bones:
- **Maxillary** (cheek), the largest
- **Frontal** (forehead)
- **Ethmoid** (a honeycomb of small cells between the eyes)
- **Sphenoid** (deep, behind the nose)

They are lined by **respiratory mucosa**: tiny hair-like cilia sweep mucus toward each sinus opening, called an **ostium**. Most sinuses drain into the **middle meatus**. The sphenoid drains above the superior concha. The **nasolacrimal duct**, which carries tears, opens into the inferior meatus. That is why crying gives you a runny nose.

The roof of the nose is the thin **cribriform plate**, where smell nerves pass up to the brain.

Real example: in **sinusitis**, swollen lining blocks an ostium. Mucus pools and can become infected, causing facial pressure and congestion.
levels.college:
**Walls of the nasal cavity**
- Roof: nasal and frontal bones, the **cribriform plate of the ethmoid**, and the body of the sphenoid. The olfactory nerve (CN I) fibers pass through the cribriform plate.
- Floor: palatine process of the maxilla and the horizontal plate of the palatine bone (the hard palate).
- Medial wall (septum): septal cartilage, the **perpendicular plate of the ethmoid**, and the **vomer**.
- Lateral wall: the superior and middle conchae (parts of the ethmoid), the inferior concha (a separate bone), plus the maxilla, lacrimal bone and perpendicular plate of the palatine.

**Drainage map**
- **Sphenoethmoidal recess** (above the superior concha): sphenoid sinus.
- **Superior meatus**: posterior ethmoid cells.
- **Middle meatus**: frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoid sinuses. Under the middle concha sits the **ethmoidal bulla**, a large anterior ethmoid cell that bulges inward. Below it is a curved cleft, the **semilunar hiatus**, and the **hiatus semilunaris** leads into the **ethmoidal infundibulum**. The frontal sinus drains via the **frontonasal duct/recess**. Middle ethmoid cells open on the bulla.
- **Inferior meatus**: nasolacrimal duct, guarded by the valve of Hasner.

The maxillary ostium sits in the upper part of the sinus's medial wall, so gravity works against drainage. Clearance depends on **mucociliary transport**.

**Nerves**
- Smell: CN I, from the olfactory epithelium in the roof.
- General sensation: CN V1 (anterior ethmoidal nerve) supplies the front and upper part. CN V2 (nasopalatine and posterior lateral nasal branches via the **pterygopalatine ganglion**) supplies most of the rest.
- Glands: parasympathetic fibers from CN VII (greater petrosal nerve, through the nerve of the pterygoid canal) synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion.

**Arteries**: sphenopalatine (from the maxillary artery), anterior and posterior ethmoidal (from the ophthalmic artery), greater palatine, and the septal branch of the superior labial (from the facial artery). These meet on the anterior septum at **Kiesselbach's plexus** (Little's area), the site of most nosebleeds.
levels.phd:
**Ostiomeatal complex (OMC).** The functional drainage unit of the anterior sinuses is the **ostiomeatal complex**: the uncinate process, ethmoidal infundibulum, hiatus semilunaris, ethmoidal bulla, middle meatus and frontal recess. Small mucosal swellings here can obstruct the frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoid sinuses at once. This idea, developed by Messerklinger's endoscopic studies of mucociliary flow and popularized by Stammberger and Kennedy, is the anatomical basis of **functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS)**.

**Mucociliary clearance.** Ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium beats at roughly 10 to 15 Hz in a periciliary sol layer, under a gel mucus blanket. Messerklinger showed that clearance follows fixed routes toward the natural ostium, even when a second (accessory) opening exists. This explains **recirculation**: mucus can leave through the natural ostium and re-enter through an accessory or surgically made opening. Impaired cilia (primary ciliary dyskinesia, Kartagener syndrome) or abnormal mucus (cystic fibrosis, caused by CFTR mutations) produce chronic sinus disease.

**Anatomical variants that narrow drainage**
- **Agger nasi cell**: the most anterior ethmoid cell; it shapes the frontal recess.
- **Haller (infraorbital ethmoid) cells**: can narrow the infundibulum.
- **Concha bullosa**: a pneumatized middle concha.
- **Paradoxical middle concha** and septal deviation.
- **Onodi (sphenoethmoidal) cell**: a posterior ethmoid cell that extends lateral or superior to the sphenoid sinus and can contain the optic nerve.

**Development.** The maxillary and ethmoid sinuses are present at birth. The frontal sinus is rarely visible on radiographs before about age 6 and keeps enlarging into adolescence. Sphenoid pneumatization expands through childhood and is classified as conchal, presellar or sellar, with sellar being most common in adults. That pattern decides whether a transsphenoidal route to the pituitary is easy.

**Nasal cycle.** Venous sinusoids in the inferior conchae fill and empty in alternation between sides under autonomic control. Sympathetic tone shrinks them. This erectile tissue is why decongestant effects and rebound congestion matter physiologically.

**Nitric oxide.** The sinuses produce large amounts of nitric oxide (through NOS2), which has antimicrobial effects and may help ventilation-perfusion matching. This is one proposed function of sinuses, alongside humidification and lightening the skull. Their true evolutionary purpose remains debated.
levels.expert:
**The endoscopic skull base corridor.** For a neurosurgeon, the nose is an operating corridor. The **endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal approach** reaches the sella through the sphenoid rostrum. Wider routes (transplanum, transtuberculum, transclival, transcribriform) reach the anterior skull base and clivus. Landmarks on the sphenoid lateral wall include the **opticocarotid recess** (lateral OCR), the carotid and optic protuberances, and the sellar floor. Septation of the sphenoid sinus often inserts onto the carotid prominence, so twisting or fracturing those septa risks injury to the internal carotid artery (ICA). Dehiscent bone over the ICA or optic nerve is common enough that a preoperative CT review is essential.

**CT checklist before sinus or skull base surgery** (the CLOSE mnemonic):
- **C**ribriform plate: **Keros classification** of olfactory fossa depth (type I about 1 to 3 mm, II 4 to 7, III 8 to 16). Type III and asymmetric lateral lamellae carry the greatest risk of CSF leak, because the lateral lamella is the thinnest bone of the anterior skull base.
- **L**amina papyracea: dehiscence risks orbital entry, hematoma or medial rectus injury.
- **O**nodi cells: they bring the optic nerve into the posterior ethmoid.
- **S**phenoid: pneumatization type and septal insertions.
- **E**thmoidal arteries: an anterior ethmoidal artery hanging free in a mesentery below the skull base can retract into the orbit if cut, producing a retrobulbar hematoma.

**Reconstruction.** The **Hadad-Bassagasteguy nasoseptal flap**, pedicled on the posterior septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery, cut postoperative CSF leak rates after extended endonasal surgery from substantial levels to low single digits. It must be harvested before posterior septectomy, or its pedicle may be lost.

**Pitfalls in practice**
- **Posterior epistaxis** from sphenopalatine territory often fails anterior packing. Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation, at the crista ethmoidalis, is the definitive option.
- Unilateral clear rhinorrhea after trauma or surgery is a CSF leak until proven otherwise. **Beta-2 transferrin** or beta-trace protein testing confirms it.
- Unilateral nasal obstruction with epistaxis in an adolescent male suggests **juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma**, which arises near the sphenopalatine foramen.

**Open questions** include the role of the microbiome and type 2 inflammation in chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, now targeted by biologics such as dupilumab. Another is how best to preserve olfaction and nasal function during extended endonasal approaches.

keyPoints: The septum (septal cartilage, ethmoid perpendicular plate, vomer) divides the nasal cavity
Three conchae overlie meatuses, which are the drainage channels
Frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoid sinuses drain to the middle meatus via the ostiomeatal complex
Sphenoid drains to the sphenoethmoidal recess; nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus
Mucociliary clearance moves mucus toward natural ostia, so blocked ostia cause sinusitis
Kiesselbach's plexus causes most nosebleeds; the sphenopalatine artery causes posterior bleeds

test.q: Where does the sphenoid sinus drain?
choices: Middle meatus below the middle concha
Inferior meatus below the inferior concha
Superior meatus below the superior concha
test.explain: The sphenoid opens into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha. The posterior ethmoid cells, not the sphenoid, drain into the superior meatus.

test.q: The nasolacrimal duct opens into which space?
test.explain: Tears drain through the nasolacrimal duct into the inferior meatus. This is why crying causes a runny nose.

test.q: Which bone is part of the nasal septum?
test.explain: The septum is formed by septal cartilage, the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, and the vomer. The lacrimal bone and inferior concha belong to the lateral wall.

test.q: Which sinus is the largest?
test.explain: The maxillary sinus, in the cheek, is the largest paranasal sinus.

test.q: Why does the maxillary sinus drain poorly when you are upright?
choices: Its lining has no working cilia
Its ostium sits near the top of the sinus
Its opening lies in the cribriform plate
It drains through the inferior meatus
test.explain: The ostium is in the upper part of the medial wall, so gravity does not help. Clearance relies on cilia sweeping mucus upward.

test.q: Most anterior nosebleeds come from:
test.explain: Kiesselbach's plexus (Little's area) on the anterior septum is where several arteries meet. It is the commonest bleeding site.

test.q: Which sinuses share drainage through the ostiomeatal complex?
test.explain: The frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoid sinuses all drain into the middle meatus. Blockage there can affect all three.

test.q: Parasympathetic fibers to nasal glands synapse in the:
test.explain: Fibers from CN VII travel in the greater petrosal nerve and synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion.

test.q: Fibers of CN I reach the brain by passing through the:
test.explain: Olfactory fibers pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid in the roof of the nasal cavity.

test.q: The curled bones on the lateral nasal wall are called turbinates or ___.
test.explain: There are superior, middle and inferior conchae.

test.q: What is the name for an opening through which a sinus drains?
test.explain: Each sinus drains through an ostium (plural ostia).

test.q: The curved cleft below the ethmoidal bulla is the hiatus ___.
test.explain: The hiatus semilunaris leads into the ethmoidal infundibulum in the middle meatus.

kidTest.q: What do the curly shelves inside your nose do?
kidTest.explain: They work like radiators, warming air and making it damp.

kidTest.q: What are sinuses?
kidTest.explain: Sinuses are hollow caves full of air inside the bones of your face.

kidTest.q: Why does your face feel stuffy during a cold?
kidTest.explain: Swelling blocks the tiny doors, so mucus gets stuck.

kidTest.q: What divides the nose into two sides?
kidTest.explain: A thin wall down the middle splits the nasal cavity in two.

kidTest.q: Sinuses make your head lighter and help your v _ _ _ _ sound full.
kidTest.explain: Air-filled sinuses help your voice sound full.

advancedTest.q: After surgery creates an accessory maxillary opening, symptoms persist and mucus re-enters the sinus. The best explanation is:
choices: Gravity drains mucus out through the new opening
The inferior concha blocks the sphenoethmoidal recess
The nasolacrimal duct refluxes tears into the sinus
Cilia carry mucus to the natural ostium, causing recirculation
advancedTest.explain: Messerklinger showed that clearance heads to the natural ostium regardless of other openings. Mucus can exit and re-enter through the accessory opening.

advancedTest.q: Before ethmoidectomy, CT shows a Keros type III olfactory fossa. The main concern is:
choices: CSF leak through the lateral lamella
advancedTest.explain: A deep olfactory fossa means a tall, thin lateral lamella, which is easy to breach and can cause a CSF leak.

advancedTest.q: A transsphenoidal pituitary approach is planned. Which finding most raises the risk of optic nerve injury?
choices: A Haller cell under the orbit
An Onodi cell beside the sphenoid
advancedTest.explain: An Onodi cell extends lateral or superior to the sphenoid and can contain the optic nerve. The other cells sit farther forward or lower.

advancedTest.q: Why is the nasoseptal flap harvested before posterior septectomy?
choices: The septectomy can cut its vascular pedicle
The flap shrinks after sphenoid drilling
The septum then loses its olfactory fibers
The nasolacrimal duct blocks the flap later
advancedTest.explain: The flap depends on the posterior septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery. Posterior septectomy can sever this branch.

lessons.title: External, Middle & Inner Ear Within the Temporal Bone

levels.kid:
Your ear is like a house with three rooms, all tucked inside a hard bone on the side of your head.

The **outer ear** is the part you can see, plus a little tunnel. Sound travels down the tunnel and hits the **eardrum**, a thin skin stretched tight like a drum.

Behind the eardrum is the **middle ear**, a tiny air room with three of the smallest bones in your body. They pass the wiggles along like a chain of friends passing a message.

The **inner ear** is a snail-shaped tube filled with liquid. Tiny hair cells there turn the wiggles into signals for your brain. Next door are curly loops that help you keep your balance, so you don't tip over when you spin!
levels.hs:
The ear has three parts, and all but the outer flap sit inside the **temporal bone**, especially its dense **petrous part**.

- **External ear**: the **auricle** (pinna) collects sound and funnels it down the **external acoustic meatus** (ear canal), about 2.5 cm long, to the **tympanic membrane** (eardrum).
- **Middle ear (tympanic cavity)**: an air-filled space holding three **ossicles**: the **malleus** (hammer), **incus** (anvil) and **stapes** (stirrup). The stapes footplate sits in the **oval window** of the inner ear. The **Eustachian (pharyngotympanic) tube** links the middle ear to the throat to equalize pressure. That is why your ears "pop" on a plane.
- **Inner ear**: a fluid-filled **bony labyrinth** containing the **cochlea** (hearing), the **vestibule** and three **semicircular canals** (balance).

The ossicles act as a lever and pressure booster. Sound in air would mostly bounce off fluid, so the middle ear concentrates the force from the big eardrum onto the tiny oval window.

Real example: **otitis media**, a middle-ear infection common in children, happens partly because a child's Eustachian tube is shorter and more horizontal, so fluid drains poorly. Two nerves, the **facial (CN VII)** and **vestibulocochlear (CN VIII)**, enter the temporal bone through the **internal acoustic meatus**.
levels.college:
**External ear.** The auricle is elastic cartilage covered by skin. The lobule has no cartilage. The external acoustic meatus is S-shaped. Its lateral third is cartilaginous and its medial two-thirds are bony. Sensory supply is mixed: the **auriculotemporal nerve (V3)**, the **great auricular nerve (C2–C3)**, the **auricular branch of the vagus** (Arnold's nerve, which explains the cough reflex when the canal is cleaned) and twigs of VII. The tympanic membrane has a lax **pars flaccida** above and a tense **pars tensa** below. Its center (umbo) is pulled in by the handle of the malleus. Viewed through an otoscope, the **cone of light** points anteroinferiorly.

**Middle ear walls** (a useful box model):
- Roof (tegmental): **tegmen tympani**, a thin plate separating the ear from the middle cranial fossa.
- Floor (jugular): the bone over the **internal jugular vein**.
- Lateral (membranous): the tympanic membrane.
- Medial (labyrinthine): the **promontory** (basal turn of the cochlea), the oval and round windows, and the bulge of the facial canal.
- Anterior (carotid): the internal carotid artery, the Eustachian tube and the tensor tympani.
- Posterior (mastoid): the **aditus** to the mastoid antrum, and the pyramidal eminence housing the stapedius.

**Muscles.** **Tensor tympani** (V3) and **stapedius** (VII) damp loud sounds. Stapedius paralysis in a facial palsy causes **hyperacusis**.

**Nerves crossing the middle ear.** The **tympanic plexus** comes from CN IX (Jacobson's nerve) and gives rise to the lesser petrosal nerve, which carries parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland. The **chorda tympani** (VII) runs between malleus and incus, carrying taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

**Inner ear.** The bony labyrinth contains **perilymph** (rich in Na⁺). Inside it, the membranous labyrinth contains **endolymph** (rich in K⁺). The cochlea makes about 2.75 turns around the **modiolus**. The **organ of Corti** sits on the basilar membrane. The utricle and saccule sense linear acceleration. The semicircular canals sense rotation.
levels.phd:
**Impedance matching.** The middle ear offsets the roughly 30 dB transmission loss at an air–fluid boundary. Most of the gain comes from the area ratio of the tympanic membrane to the stapes footplate (effective areas of about 55 mm² versus 3.2 mm², roughly 17:1). The ossicular lever adds about 1.3:1 more. Round-window compliance is essential: the cochlear fluid is incompressible, so the oval and round windows must move in opposite phase. If both windows are driven equally, little traveling wave forms.

**Cochlear mechanics.** Von Békésy (Nobel Prize 1961) showed that a **traveling wave** runs along the basilar membrane. Its tonotopy is set by gradients in membrane stiffness and width: high frequencies are sensed at the base, low frequencies at the apex. The sharp tuning of living cochleae, however, depends on the **cochlear amplifier**. **Outer hair cells** change length through **prestin** (SLC26A5) electromotility. Their activity produces **otoacoustic emissions** (Kemp, 1978).

**Transduction.** Stereocilia deflection opens **mechanoelectrical transduction (MET) channels** at the tips, gated by **tip links** made of cadherin-23 and protocadherin-15. The channel core includes **TMC1/TMC2**. The driving force is large because endolymph is K⁺-rich and sits at an **endocochlear potential** of about +80 mV, generated by the **stria vascularis**. The stria pumps K⁺ through Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and NKCC1 and recycles it through gap junctions built from connexin-26 (GJB2). GJB2 mutations are the most common cause of nonsyndromic genetic deafness. About 95% of afferent fibers in the spiral ganglion (type I) contact **inner hair cells**.

**Facial nerve course in the temporal bone.** The nerve has internal meatal, labyrinthine, tympanic and mastoid segments. The labyrinthine segment is the narrowest point (the meatal foramen, under about 0.7 mm wide), which may explain why swelling compresses it in Bell's palsy. At the **geniculate ganglion** the greater petrosal nerve branches off. The nerve then gives the stapedius and the chorda tympani, and exits at the **stylomastoid foramen**.

**Endolymph homeostasis.** The **endolymphatic duct and sac** pass through the vestibular aqueduct. **Endolymphatic hydrops** is the pathological hallmark of **Ménière's disease**, though whether hydrops causes the symptoms or merely accompanies them is still debated.
levels.expert:
For the skull-base surgeon, the temporal bone is a 3D maze of landmarks rather than a list of ear parts.

- **Translabyrinthine and retrosigmoid routes** to vestibular schwannomas trade hearing preservation against exposure. In the internal acoustic meatus, the facial nerve lies anterosuperior, with the cochlear nerve anteroinferior and the two vestibular nerves posterior. The mnemonic is "Seven-Up, Coke Down." **Bill's bar**, a vertical crest at the fundus, separates the facial nerve from the superior vestibular nerve. Tumors usually displace the facial nerve anteriorly, where it becomes a thin ribbon.
- **Arcuate eminence** and **tegmen** guide the middle fossa approach. The arcuate eminence only loosely corresponds to the superior canal. **Superior canal dehiscence** (Minor, 1998) creates a "third window" in the labyrinth. It produces sound- or pressure-induced vertigo (Tullio phenomenon), autophony, and conductive hyperacusis with bone-conduction thresholds better than normal. Thin-slice CT reformatted in the Pöschl plane is the diagnostic standard.
- **Mastoid landmarks**: **Trautmann's triangle**, the sigmoid sinus, the lateral (horizontal) canal and the digastric ridge locate the vertical facial nerve segment. A **dehiscent tympanic segment** of the facial canal is reported in a substantial fraction of temporal bones, so the nerve is at risk in middle-ear surgery.

**Temporal bone fractures.** The older classification (longitudinal vs transverse) has given way to **otic capsule-sparing vs otic capsule-violating** fractures. The newer scheme predicts outcomes better: capsule-violating fractures carry substantially higher risks of sensorineural loss, facial palsy and CSF leak.

**Pharmacology at the cochlea.** Aminoglycosides enter hair cells through MET channels. They cause ototoxicity, which is worsened by the mitochondrial **m.1555A>G** variant in MT-RNR1. Cisplatin is also ototoxic. **Sodium thiosulfate** is now approved to reduce cisplatin hearing loss in pediatric solid tumors. Intratympanic steroids and gentamicin exploit round-window permeability.

**Frontiers.** **Hidden hearing loss** (cochlear synaptopathy; Kujawa and Liberman, 2009) is loss of ribbon synapses with normal audiometric thresholds. Its importance in humans is still debated. AAV gene therapy for **OTOF**-related deafness restored hearing in early trials reported in 2024. Improved cochlear implant electrode designs aim to preserve residual hearing.

keyPoints: External, middle and inner ear lie within the temporal bone (petrous part for inner ear)
Ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) match air-to-fluid impedance, mainly via the eardrum-to-footplate area ratio
Middle ear walls: tegmen roof, jugular floor, promontory medial, carotid anterior, mastoid posterior
Chorda tympani and tympanic plexus (CN IX) cross the middle ear; stapedius (VII) and tensor tympani (V3) damp sound
Cochlea transduces via hair cells bathed in K+-rich endolymph; semicircular canals and otoliths sense balance
Facial nerve runs a labyrinthine, tympanic and mastoid course, exiting at the stylomastoid foramen

test.q: Which ossicle's footplate sits in the oval window?
test.explain: The stapes footplate fits into the oval window and transmits vibration to the perilymph. The modiolus is the bony core of the cochlea, not an ossicle.

test.q: Why do children get middle-ear infections more easily than adults?
choices: Their auditory tube is short and horizontal
Their eardrum has no tense lower pars tensa
Their ear canal is bony along its full length
Their cochlea holds more sodium-rich perilymph
test.explain: A short, horizontal Eustachian tube drains the middle ear poorly, so fluid collects and becomes infected.

test.q: The roof of the middle ear, separating it from the middle cranial fossa, is the:
test.explain: The tegmen tympani is a thin bony plate forming the roof. The promontory lies on the medial wall.

test.q: Paralysis of which muscle causes hyperacusis in facial nerve palsy?
test.explain: Stapedius is supplied by CN VII and damps stapes movement. Tensor tympani is supplied by V3, so it is spared in facial palsy.

test.q: Which nerve passes between the malleus and incus carrying taste fibers?
test.explain: The chorda tympani, a branch of VII, crosses the middle ear carrying taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

test.q: Coughing when the ear canal is cleaned is due to stimulation of:
choices: The auricular branch of the vagus
test.explain: Arnold's nerve (the auricular branch of CN X) supplies part of the canal, which triggers a vagal cough reflex.

test.q: The main source of the middle ear's pressure gain is:
choices: The curved shape of the auricle
The fluid in the semicircular canals
The length of the ear canal
test.explain: Concentrating force from the large tympanic membrane onto the small footplate supplies most of the gain. The ossicular lever adds a little more.

test.q: Which structures detect rotation of the head?
test.explain: The three semicircular canals sense rotation. The utricle and saccule sense linear acceleration.

test.q: The bulge on the medial wall of the middle ear formed by the cochlea's basal turn is the:
test.explain: The promontory is formed by the basal turn of the cochlea. The umbo is the center of the eardrum.

test.q: Which fluid, rich in potassium, fills the membranous labyrinth?
test.explain: Endolymph is K⁺-rich. Perilymph, in the bony labyrinth around it, is Na⁺-rich.

test.q: The facial nerve leaves the skull through the ___ foramen.
test.explain: After its temporal bone course, CN VII exits at the stylomastoid foramen.

test.q: What is the other name for the pharyngotympanic tube?
test.explain: It connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx and equalizes pressure.

kidTest.q: What is the eardrum like?
choices: A small, hard piece of bone
A long tube filled with water
kidTest.explain: The eardrum is thin and tight, like the top of a drum.

kidTest.q: What is in the middle ear?
choices: Big ear muscles you can feel
kidTest.explain: The middle ear holds three tiny bones that pass sound along.

kidTest.q: What shape is the hearing part of the inner ear?
kidTest.explain: The cochlea is curled like a snail shell.

kidTest.q: What do the curly loops in the inner ear help with?
kidTest.explain: The loops sense spinning so you don't tip over.

kidTest.q: Tiny ___ cells turn wiggles into brain signals. Hint: h _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Hair cells in the inner ear change sound wiggles into signals for the brain.

advancedTest.q: If a lesion let sound reach the oval and round windows equally and in phase, hearing would drop mainly because:
choices: Stapedius would stop damping the louder sounds
The endocochlear potential would collapse to zero
Tip links would detach from the stereocilia
Incompressible fluid needs opposite window motion
advancedTest.explain: Cochlear fluid can't compress, so a traveling wave needs the round window to bulge out when the oval window moves in. In-phase drive cancels this motion.

advancedTest.q: Superior canal dehiscence gives bone-conduction thresholds better than normal because it:
choices: Adds a third mobile window to the labyrinth
advancedTest.explain: The extra window shunts energy and lowers labyrinthine impedance, which improves bone conduction and causes an apparent conductive loss.

advancedTest.q: Why are aminoglycosides selectively toxic to hair cells?
choices: They bind connexin-26 in the stapes
They block the stria's Na+/K+ pump
They are taken up through MET channels
advancedTest.explain: Aminoglycosides enter hair cells through mechanotransduction channels. The m.1555A>G variant raises susceptibility.

advancedTest.q: A transverse-looking temporal bone fracture is described today mainly by whether it:
choices: Runs parallel to the petrous ridge
advancedTest.explain: Capsule-violating versus capsule-sparing status predicts sensorineural loss, facial palsy and CSF leak better than the old longitudinal/transverse scheme.

lessons.title: Oral Cavity, Tongue & the Salivary Glands

levels.kid:
Your mouth is like a busy kitchen. Your teeth are the choppers. Your tongue is the mixer. It pushes food around and tastes it too!

Your tongue is a big bundle of muscles. It can bend, curl and poke because the muscles point in different directions.

Your mouth also has little juice factories called **salivary glands**. They make spit, or saliva. There are three big pairs: one in front of each ear, one under the jaw, and one under the tongue. Saliva makes food wet and slippery so it slides down easily. It even starts breaking down bread before you swallow!

Tiny wires called **nerves** tell the tongue how to move. Other nerves tell your brain what tastes sweet or salty.
levels.hs:
The **oral cavity** runs from the lips back to the **palatoglossal arches**, the folds at the back of the mouth. Behind them lies the throat. The oral cavity has two parts. The **vestibule** is the space between the cheeks and the teeth. The **oral cavity proper** lies inside the teeth. The roof is the **palate**: a bony **hard palate** in front and a muscular **soft palate** behind. The soft palate rises to seal off the nose when you swallow.

The **tongue** is made almost entirely of skeletal muscle. **Intrinsic muscles** change its shape. **Extrinsic muscles** attach it to bone and move it around. Its front two-thirds and back third differ in development and in nerve supply.

There are three paired major **salivary glands**:
- **Parotid**: largest, in front of the ear. It makes watery saliva rich in **amylase**, an enzyme that starts digesting starch. Its duct opens beside the upper second molar.
- **Submandibular**: under the jaw. It makes the most saliva at rest.
- **Sublingual**: under the tongue. It is the smallest and makes mucus-rich saliva.

A real example: salivary stones (**sialolithiasis**) most often form in the submandibular gland. Its saliva is thicker and its duct runs uphill, so a stone can block it. The gland then swells painfully at mealtimes.
levels.college:
**Boundaries.** The oral cavity proper is bounded by the palate above, the mylohyoid and tongue below, and the cheeks laterally. It opens into the oropharynx at the palatoglossal arches. The hard palate is formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones. The soft palate is moved by five muscles: tensor veli palatini (supplied by CN V3), and levator veli palatini, palatoglossus, palatopharyngeus and musculus uvulae (all supplied by the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus).

**Tongue structure.** The **terminal sulcus** and **foramen cecum**, the remnant of the thyroid's descent, divide the oral two-thirds from the pharyngeal third. The **vallate papillae** sit just in front of the sulcus.

**Tongue muscles.**
- Intrinsic muscles (longitudinal, transverse, vertical) change shape.
- Extrinsic muscles move the tongue: **genioglossus** (protrudes), **hyoglossus** (depresses), **styloglossus** (retracts and elevates) and palatoglossus (elevates the back).
- All are supplied by the **hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)** except palatoglossus, which is supplied by the vagus.

**Tongue sensation.**
- Anterior two-thirds: general sensation by the **lingual nerve** (V3); taste by the **chorda tympani** (VII).
- Posterior third: both general sensation and taste by the **glossopharyngeal nerve** (IX).
- Epiglottic region: vagus via the internal laryngeal nerve.

**Salivary glands.**
- **Parotid**: serous saliva. Its duct (**Stensen's**) pierces the buccinator. Parasympathetic supply: IX → lesser petrosal nerve → **otic ganglion** → auriculotemporal nerve.
- **Submandibular**: mixed saliva, about 70% of resting flow. It wraps around the posterior edge of mylohyoid. Its duct (**Wharton's**) opens at the sublingual caruncle.
- **Sublingual**: mainly mucous saliva. It drains through many small ducts (of Rivinus).
- Submandibular and sublingual parasympathetic supply: VII → chorda tympani → lingual nerve → **submandibular ganglion**.

Sympathetic fibres come from the superior cervical ganglion and travel along the arteries. They produce a small volume of protein-rich saliva.

**Clinical check.** Ask the patient to stick out the tongue. With a CN XII lesion, the tongue deviates toward the weak side, because the healthy genioglossus pushes unopposed.
levels.phd:
**Embryology explains the innervation.** The anterior tongue arises from the median tongue bud (tuberculum impar) and the paired lateral lingual swellings of pharyngeal arch 1. Hence its general sensation comes from V3. Taste is carried by the chorda tympani, an arch 2 nerve that hitchhikes on the lingual nerve.

The posterior tongue comes from the copula and hypopharyngeal eminence, which are arch 3 and arch 4 derivatives. The arch 3 portion overgrows arch 2, which explains the glossopharyngeal dominance there. The muscles, by contrast, derive from **occipital somites** that migrate forward dragging CN XII. This is why a somatic motor nerve, not an arch nerve, moves the tongue.

**Taste pathway.** Taste receptor cells sit in buds on fungiform, foliate and vallate papillae.
- Sweet, umami and bitter use GPCRs: T1R2/T1R3, T1R1/T1R3 and the T2R family. These signal through gustducin, PLCβ2, IP3 and the cation channel TRPM5. The cells release ATP through CALHM1/3 channels onto P2X2/P2X3 receptors on afferent fibres.
- Sour depends on the proton channel **OTOP1**.
- Low-salt taste depends on the amiloride-sensitive ENaC.
- Afferents from VII, IX and X converge on the rostral **nucleus of the solitary tract**, then project to the ventral posteromedial thalamus and the insular/opercular gustatory cortex.
- The "tongue map" of regional taste zones is a misreading of Hänig (1901). All taste qualities are detected across all taste-bud fields.

**Secretion mechanism.** Saliva is made in two stages.
- Acinar cells secrete an isotonic primary fluid. Acetylcholine acts on M3 receptors, raising calcium, which opens apical TMEM16A chloride channels. Basolateral NKCC1 supplies the chloride.
- Striated and intercalated ducts then reabsorb Na⁺ and Cl⁻ and secrete K⁺ and HCO₃⁻, while staying relatively water-impermeable. Final saliva is therefore **hypotonic**.
- At high flow there is less time for ductal modification, so Na⁺ and tonicity rise.
- β-adrenergic cAMP signalling triggers exocytosis of amylase-rich granules.
- Aquaporin-5 mediates acinar water flux and is mislocalized in Sjögren's syndrome.

Blood supply: the **lingual artery** runs deep to hyoglossus, whereas the hypoglossal nerve and the submandibular duct run superficial to it. That layering is the classic anatomical key to the floor of the mouth.
levels.expert:
**Floor-of-mouth surgery.** The lingual nerve loops beneath Wharton's duct, crossing lateral, then inferior, then medial to it. This makes it vulnerable during submandibular gland excision and stone removal through the mouth. In the neck, the marginal mandibular branch of VII runs superficial to the gland's capsule within investing fascia. Surgeons protect it with the Hayes Martin manoeuvre, ligating the facial vein low and retracting it upward.

The lingual nerve also lies just medial to the lower third molar socket, sometimes above the alveolar crest. Lower wisdom-tooth extraction carries a small risk of lingual paresthesia and taste loss.

**Ludwig's angina** is bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces, usually from an infected lower molar. Its importance comes from geometry: lower molar roots lie below the mylohyoid line, mylohyoid forms the floor, and the infection pushes the tongue up and back. The airway, not antibiotic choice, is the dominant concern. Awake fibreoptic intubation or surgical airway planning is standard.

**Hypoglossal nerve.**
- At the skull base, it exits through the hypoglossal canal. Craniovertebral junction tumours, condylar fractures and anterior C1–C2 approaches can injure it.
- Fasciculations and atrophy suggest a lower motor neuron lesion, such as motor neuron disease.
- A supranuclear lesion gives milder deviation, toward the side opposite the lesion.
- **Hypoglossal nerve stimulation** (an upper-airway stimulator acting on genioglossus) is an established therapy for selected obstructive sleep apnea patients who cannot tolerate CPAP. It selectively recruits protrusor branches.
- Hypoglossal-facial anastomosis remains a reanimation option after facial nerve loss, at the cost of some tongue function.

**Salivary gland disease and treatment.**
- Tumour rule of thumb: the smaller the gland, the more likely a tumour is malignant. About 20–25% of parotid tumours, ~40–50% of submandibular tumours and most sublingual tumours are malignant.
- Adenoid cystic carcinoma shows characteristic perineural spread, including along V3 to the skull base.
- Sialendoscopy now allows gland-preserving stone removal.
- Radiation-induced xerostomia drives parotid-sparing IMRT.
- Phase 1 trials of AQP1 gene transfer have shown preliminary improvement in salivary flow in some irradiated patients.
- Pharmacology link: anticholinergic burden and M3 agonists (pilocarpine, cevimeline, used for Sjögren's dryness) show the muscarinic control of salivation directly.

**Open questions** include acinar stem/progenitor cell regeneration and the role of fat taste receptors (CD36, GPR120).

keyPoints: Oral cavity ends at the palatoglossal arches; vestibule vs oral cavity proper
All tongue muscles are supplied by CN XII except palatoglossus (vagus)
Anterior 2/3: touch by lingual (V3), taste by chorda tympani (VII); posterior 1/3: CN IX
Parotid (serous, Stensen's duct, otic ganglion via IX)
Submandibular and sublingual glands get VII parasympathetic fibres via the submandibular ganglion
Saliva starts isotonic in acini and becomes hypotonic in ducts; M3 receptors drive secretion

test.q: Which tongue muscle is NOT supplied by the hypoglossal nerve?
test.explain: Palatoglossus is supplied by the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus. All other tongue muscles are supplied by CN XII.

test.q: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue travels in which nerve?
test.explain: Chorda tympani (VII) carries anterior taste, riding on the lingual nerve. The lingual nerve itself carries general sensation.

test.q: Where does the parotid duct open?
test.explain: Stensen's duct pierces buccinator and opens opposite the upper second molar. Wharton's duct opens at the sublingual caruncle.

test.q: Which ganglion relays parasympathetic fibres to the parotid?
test.explain: IX → lesser petrosal → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve → parotid.

test.q: Salivary stones most often form in which gland?
test.explain: Thicker saliva and an uphill-running duct favour stones in the submandibular gland.

test.q: A patient's protruded tongue deviates to the left. A lower motor neuron lesion is most likely in:
test.explain: The intact right genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the weak left side.

test.q: Which soft palate muscle is supplied by CN V3?
test.explain: Tensor veli palatini is supplied by V3. The other palate muscles are supplied by the vagus.

test.q: Which gland produces the most saliva at rest?
test.explain: The submandibular gland provides about 70% of resting flow. The parotid dominates during stimulated flow.

test.q: General sensation and taste of the posterior third of the tongue come from:
test.explain: CN IX supplies both modalities to the posterior third.

test.q: Name the starch-digesting enzyme abundant in parotid saliva.
test.explain: Serous parotid saliva is rich in amylase.

test.q: The space between the cheeks and the teeth is the oral ___.
test.explain: The vestibule lies outside the teeth; the oral cavity proper lies inside them.

test.q: What is the eponym for the submandibular duct?
test.explain: Wharton's duct opens at the sublingual caruncle.

kidTest.q: What do salivary glands make?
kidTest.explain: Salivary glands make spit, called saliva.

kidTest.q: What is the tongue mostly made of?
kidTest.explain: The tongue is a bundle of muscles.

kidTest.q: Where is the biggest salivary gland?
kidTest.explain: The parotid sits in front of each ear.

kidTest.q: How does saliva help you eat?
kidTest.explain: Wet, slippery food slides down easily.

kidTest.q: Tiny wires that tell the tongue how to move are called n _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Nerves carry messages between the brain and the tongue.

advancedTest.q: Why is the tongue moved by CN XII rather than by a pharyngeal arch nerve?
choices: Its muscles arise from occipital somites
The muscles develop late from neural crest
Its muscles come from arch 1 mesoderm
Its muscles derive from arch 4 mesoderm
advancedTest.explain: Tongue muscles migrate forward from occipital somites with their somatic motor nerve, CN XII.

advancedTest.q: During maximal stimulated flow, saliva has higher Na⁺ than at rest because:
choices: Ducts have less time to reabsorb
advancedTest.explain: The primary fluid is isotonic; at high flow, ductal Na⁺/Cl⁻ reabsorption has less time to act.

advancedTest.q: During submandibular gland excision, which structure is most at risk where it loops beneath the duct?
advancedTest.explain: The lingual nerve crosses lateral, inferior, then medial to Wharton's duct.

advancedTest.q: In Ludwig's angina, why do lower molar infections reach the submandibular space?
choices: Their roots lie below the mylohyoid line
They spread via the pterygoid plexus
They drain into the parotid capsule
advancedTest.explain: Roots below the mylohyoid attachment open into the submandibular space.

lessons.title: Pharynx and Larynx: Muscles, Cartilages & Innervation

levels.kid:
At the back of your mouth is a muscly tube called the **pharynx**, or throat. Food and air both travel through it. Then the road splits. Food goes back into a tube to your stomach. Air goes forward into your **larynx**, the voice box.

The larynx is like a little box built from stiff pieces called cartilages. The bump on the front of some people's necks, the Adam's apple, is one of them. Inside are two **vocal folds**. When air rushes past, they wiggle like guitar strings and make your voice.

When you swallow, a flap called the **epiglottis** folds down like a lid. Your voice box also lifts up and squeezes shut. That keeps food out of your lungs. Tiny nerves control all of this.
levels.hs:
The **pharynx** is a muscular tube about 12-14 cm long. It runs from the base of the skull to the level of the cricoid cartilage, roughly at the sixth cervical vertebra (C6). It has three parts:
- **Nasopharynx**: behind the nose, carries air only.
- **Oropharynx**: behind the mouth, where the tonsils sit.
- **Laryngopharynx** (hypopharynx): behind the larynx. It leads into the esophagus.

Three **constrictor muscles** (superior, middle, inferior) stack like nested cups. They squeeze food downward during swallowing.

The **larynx** protects the airway and makes the voice. Its skeleton is made of **cartilages**. The **thyroid cartilage** forms the Adam's apple. The ring-shaped **cricoid cartilage** sits below it. The two small **arytenoid cartilages** sit on top of the cricoid, and the vocal folds attach to them. The leaf-shaped **epiglottis** guards the entrance.

Almost everything here is controlled by the **vagus nerve** (cranial nerve X). Its **recurrent laryngeal nerve** loops down into the chest and climbs back up to supply most laryngeal muscles.

Real example: during thyroid surgery, this nerve lies close to the gland. If one side is injured, the patient may wake up hoarse because one vocal fold no longer moves properly.
levels.college:
**Pharyngeal wall.** The pharynx has an outer circular layer made of the superior, middle and inferior constrictors. The inferior constrictor has two parts: **thyropharyngeus** and **cricopharyngeus**, the upper esophageal sphincter. Weak spots in the wall include **Killian's dehiscence**, which lies between these two parts. This is where a **Zenker diverticulum** forms. The inner longitudinal layer is made of **stylopharyngeus**, **palatopharyngeus** and **salpingopharyngeus**, which elevate the pharynx.

**Innervation of the pharynx.** The **pharyngeal plexus** carries motor fibres from the vagus to every pharyngeal muscle except one. **Stylopharyngeus** is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). Sensation from the oropharynx comes via CN IX, which forms the afferent limb of the gag reflex. The vagus provides the efferent limb.

**Laryngeal cartilages.** There are three unpaired cartilages: thyroid, cricoid and epiglottis. There are three paired ones: arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform. The cricoid is the only complete ring in the airway.

**Intrinsic muscles and their actions:**
- **Posterior cricoarytenoid**: the *only* abductor. It opens the glottis.
- **Lateral cricoarytenoid**, **transverse and oblique arytenoids**: adduct the folds.
- **Cricothyroid**: tilts the thyroid cartilage forward. This lengthens and tenses the folds and raises pitch.
- **Thyroarytenoid / vocalis**: shortens and relaxes the folds, fine-tuning tension.

**Nerves of the larynx** (all branches of the vagus):
- **Superior laryngeal nerve**: its internal branch carries sensation above the vocal folds and pierces the thyrohyoid membrane. Its external branch supplies the cricothyroid.
- **Recurrent laryngeal nerve**: supplies all other intrinsic muscles and carries sensation below the folds. On the right it hooks under the subclavian artery. On the left it hooks under the aortic arch, near the ligamentum arteriosum.

The cough reflex triggered by food touching the supraglottis depends on the internal laryngeal nerve.
levels.phd:
**Developmental logic.** Laryngeal and pharyngeal innervation follows the pharyngeal arches. The 4th arch gives rise to the cricothyroid and the constrictors, supplied by the superior laryngeal nerve and pharyngeal branches. The 6th arch gives rise to the remaining intrinsic laryngeal muscles, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The asymmetric course of the recurrent laryngeal nerves reflects asymmetric involution of the aortic arches. On the right, the distal 6th arch artery and the 5th arch disappear, so the nerve recurs around the 4th-arch-derived subclavian artery. On the left, the persistent ductus arteriosus (6th arch) holds the nerve in the thorax. A **non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve** (about 0.5-1%) accompanies an aberrant retroesophageal right subclavian artery.

**Motor neurons.** Branchiomotor fibres arise from the **nucleus ambiguus** in the medulla. Laryngeal sensory afferents have cell bodies in the nodose (inferior vagal) ganglion and project to the **nucleus tractus solitarius**. Swallowing is organized by a medullary central pattern generator. It involves a dorsal group in and around the NTS and a ventral group near the nucleus ambiguus. The sequence was mapped classically by Doty and Bosma and by Jean.

**Vocal fold microstructure.** Hirano's **body-cover model** describes the fold in layers:
- the epithelium and superficial lamina propria (**Reinke's space**) form a pliable cover;
- the intermediate and deep lamina propria (the vocal ligament) form a transition;
- the vocalis muscle forms the body.

Phonation follows the myoelastic-aerodynamic theory. Subglottic pressure separates the folds. Then tissue elasticity and Bernoulli-related pressure drops plus inertive vocal-tract loading sustain a travelling **mucosal wave**. Fundamental frequency rises with fold tension, mainly from the cricothyroid, and with reduced effective vibrating mass.

**Position of a paralysed fold.** The Wagner-Grossman hypothesis held that isolated recurrent nerve palsy leaves the fold paramedian because the cricothyroid still adducts it. Clinical correlation is poor. Fold position depends more on synkinetic reinnervation and the degree of atrophy, so position cannot reliably localize the lesion.
levels.expert:
**Neurosurgical relevance.** In anterior cervical discectomy and fusion, postoperative dysphonia is common. Persistent recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy occurs in roughly 1-3% of cases. Proposed mechanisms include retractor compression and the rise in endotracheal cuff pressure as the larynx is displaced. Releasing and reinflating the cuff after retractor placement is a widely adopted mitigation, although trial evidence is mixed. Right- versus left-sided approaches show no consistent difference in palsy rates, despite the right nerve's shorter, more oblique course. Skull-base and foramen magnum surgery threatens the lower cranial nerves together, as in jugular foramen syndrome (IX, X, XI). Combined loss of sensation and motor function causes silent aspiration. This is far more dangerous than isolated hoarseness.

**Lesion localization.**
- A proximal vagal lesion, near the skull base or nodose ganglion, adds palatal droop, deviation of the uvula *away* from the lesion and loss of supraglottic sensation.
- An external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve injury in thyroidectomy is subtle. It causes reduced pitch range and vocal fatigue. This is classically linked to Amelita Galli-Curci, although that case is disputed. It is often missed without laryngeal electromyography.
- Bilateral recurrent nerve palsy can cause stridor and airway emergency, because both folds may lie near the midline.

**Monitoring and imaging.** Intraoperative nerve monitoring uses electromyographic endotracheal tubes. Continuous vagal stimulation can detect falling amplitude before irreversible injury. It reduces some transient palsies, but a clear reduction in permanent palsy remains unproven. For unexplained fold paralysis, imaging must cover the whole nerve course, from the skull base to the aortic arch on the left. Ortner syndrome (cardiovocal hoarseness) and apical lung tumours are classic causes.

**Therapeutic advances.** Options for unilateral paralysis include:
- injection augmentation (temporary or durable fillers);
- medialization thyroplasty (Isshiki);
- arytenoid adduction;
- selective laryngeal reinnervation, such as ansa cervicalis-to-recurrent nerve anastomosis, which restores bulk and tone, though not true abduction.

For bilateral paralysis, selective reinnervation of the posterior cricoarytenoid and implantable laryngeal pacing are emerging options, aimed at restoring inspiratory abduction.

**Open questions** include how to predict which palsies will recover, and how to protect the swallowing central pattern generator in brainstem surgery.

keyPoints: The pharynx has three parts: naso-, oro- and laryngopharynx, ending at C6/cricoid
Three constrictors squeeze food; stylopharyngeus (CN IX) is the exception to vagal supply
The cricoid is the only complete cartilage ring; arytenoids anchor the vocal folds
Posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor; cricothyroid raises pitch
Superior laryngeal nerve: sensation above the folds plus cricothyroid; recurrent nerve: the rest
Recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the subclavian (right) and aortic arch (left), so it is at risk in neck and chest surgery

test.q: Which muscle is the sole abductor of the vocal folds?
test.explain: The posterior cricoarytenoid opens the glottis. The lateral cricoarytenoid and the arytenoid muscles do the opposite: they adduct the folds.

test.q: Which pharyngeal muscle is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve?
test.explain: Stylopharyngeus is supplied by CN IX. The other pharyngeal muscles receive vagal fibres through the pharyngeal plexus.

test.q: The cricothyroid muscle is supplied by the:
choices: Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
test.explain: The cricothyroid is the one intrinsic laryngeal muscle supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, not by the recurrent nerve.

test.q: On the left side, the recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the:
test.explain: The left nerve loops under the aortic arch near the ligamentum arteriosum. On the right, it hooks under the subclavian artery.

test.q: What does contraction of the cricothyroid do to the voice?
test.explain: The cricothyroid tilts the thyroid cartilage forward, which lengthens and tenses the folds and raises pitch.

test.q: Sensation from the larynx above the vocal folds travels in the:
test.explain: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and carries sensation from above the folds. It drives the protective cough reflex.

test.q: A Zenker diverticulum forms through which weak area?
test.explain: Killian's dehiscence lies between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor.

test.q: Which part of the pharynx lies behind the larynx?
test.explain: The laryngopharynx (hypopharynx) lies behind the larynx and continues into the esophagus.

test.q: After thyroid surgery, a patient is hoarse with one immobile vocal fold. The likely injured nerve is the:
test.explain: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs close to the thyroid and supplies most intrinsic muscles, so injury leaves the fold weak or immobile.

test.q: The ___ cartilage is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway.
test.explain: The cricoid is a signet-ring shape. The tracheal rings are open at the back.

test.q: Which cranial nerve (give its name) supplies almost all muscles of the pharynx and larynx?
test.explain: The vagus (CN X) supplies them through its pharyngeal, superior laryngeal and recurrent laryngeal branches.

test.q: The cricopharyngeus forms the upper esophageal ___.
test.explain: The cricopharyngeus part of the inferior constrictor acts as the upper esophageal sphincter.

kidTest.q: What does the larynx do?
kidTest.explain: The larynx is the voice box. It also protects the airway.

kidTest.q: What flap covers the airway when you swallow?
kidTest.explain: The epiglottis folds down like a lid so food stays out of the lungs.

kidTest.q: What wiggles to make sound in your voice box?
kidTest.explain: Air rushing past the vocal folds makes them wiggle, which makes sound.

kidTest.q: Where does food go after the throat?
kidTest.explain: Food goes back into the tube that leads down to the stomach. Air goes forward into the voice box and then to the lungs.

kidTest.q: The muscly tube at the back of your mouth is the p _ _ _ _ _ x.
kidTest.explain: The pharynx, or throat, carries both food and air.

advancedTest.q: Why is a non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve associated with an aberrant retroesophageal subclavian artery?
choices: No 4th-arch-derived subclavian artery is present for the nerve to hook under
The ductus arteriosus persists on the right and pulls the nerve down
The nucleus ambiguus sends fibres down a second, separate pathway
The vagus on that side develops from the 6th arch alone
advancedTest.explain: The right nerve normally recurs around the subclavian artery, which derives from the 4th arch. If that vessel arises aberrantly, nothing drags the nerve into the chest, so it runs directly to the larynx.

advancedTest.q: A patient has hoarseness, uvula deviation and loss of supraglottic sensation. The lesion most likely lies:
choices: In the thyroid bed beside the gland
At the left aortic arch in the chest
On the vagus near the skull base
advancedTest.explain: Palatal and supraglottic sensory signs mean the pharyngeal and superior laryngeal branches are affected too. That points to a lesion on the proximal vagus, above where these branches leave it.

advancedTest.q: Why is vocal fold position after paralysis an unreliable way to localize the lesion?
choices: The cricothyroid has no effect on how the folds move
Synkinetic reinnervation and atrophy affect where the fold rests
The fold position is fixed by the cartilages alone
The posterior cricoarytenoid receives fibres from both sides
advancedTest.explain: The Wagner-Grossman prediction correlates poorly with clinical findings. Reinnervation patterns and the degree of atrophy shape fold position more than the site of the lesion.

advancedTest.q: During anterior cervical surgery, releasing and reinflating the endotracheal cuff after retractor placement aims to reduce:
choices: Pressure on the recurrent nerve from the cuff
Damage to the hypoglossal nerve from overstretching
Injury to the internal laryngeal nerve
Spasm of the cricopharyngeus during the exposure
advancedTest.explain: Retraction raises cuff pressure, which may compress intralaryngeal branches of the recurrent nerve against the displaced larynx. Reinflating the cuff afterwards lowers that pressure, although trial evidence is mixed.
